Senses.PreferredTarget: to steam sand in order to make rice
AlternateTargets: to try to cook rice from sand
SearchAliases: trying to cook sand into rice
Senses.Note: Five admitted Chinese Zen-record uses remain in one article. The full 蒸沙成飯 wording is a graph variant with the same impossible-sand-to-rice image; its only exact public citation came from excluded T48n2016.

Occurrences.Kwic: 知位次。若能依教修行，學人縱必不能自保，而教理可作保人，凡愚人作凡愚朴實語。惟望大師哀憐攝受，而卒教之。師云：台宗借用，皎如日星，自是居士錯會耳。豈不聞念空真念，生即無生？若以六識為主宰，譬如蒸沙作飯，沙非飯本。楞嚴斥能推者為心，又令微細揣摩。居士認定六識，不待別求寂常心性，正類乎認賊為子，不亦謬乎？如止觀圓頓義者，初緣實相造境，即中無不真實。從實相中出止觀二義云：法性寂然曰止，寂而常照曰
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1435.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai. Wuyi Yuanlai replies to a layman's request about using the six kinds of consciousness to know one's stage of practice. Wuyi says treating those consciousnesses as the governing source is like steaming sand to make rice, because sand is not the basis for rice. He presses the layman to act rather than rest in an intellectual classification. The headword marks the futility of using the wrong basis for the desired result.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. After a monk questions Feiyin Tongrong about an old exchange, Feiyin addresses the assembly at a meal invitation. He says that merely confining oneself for a ninety-day summer retreat and pursuing a fixed state of cessation, when treated as the Chan path itself, is like carving ice for fire or steaming sand to make rice. He contrasts that effort with a Chan person's free response in ordinary circumstances. The headword is Feiyin's own image of fruitless effort aimed at the wrong end.

Occurrences.Kwic: 林，戴高簷帽，穿厚底鞋，擊絲絛，曳長裙，以房舍穩便為安逸，飲食次第為快活，到處作模作樣，便道我是禪師，被人頂門一鎚，不覺直下粉碎。此乃是磁器禪、琉璃禪，有甚用處？是為真可憐愍者。如此修行，正是蒸沙作飯，縱經塵劫，終不能得現前。兄弟欲要急切相應，慎勿效顰此輩，只須按下雲頭，痛著精彩，勿論年月，以悟為期。況我善權山水頗佳，風景不俗，古洞幽深，長松偃蓋。喜清韻之悠揚，珍禽弄舌；樂佳味之恬淡，幽蕙
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu. Baiyu Jingsi warns his listeners against copying the clothes, comfort and manners of a Chan teacher while neglecting the work of seeing through self and reputation. He says such imitation is steaming sand to make rice: even after immense time it cannot bring realization into view. He urges the assembly to work with full attention rather than imitate those people. The headword names the impossible yield of that mistaken practice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 倒弄顛拈悉是禪，洞徹佛心無彼此，了明祖意絕中邊。雲凝壁嶂舒真印，月照寒潭露本緣，法法全彰人自昧，風吹石臼更重宣。覷破浮生夢一場，頻將身寄水雲鄉，四蛇停篋人競弄，二鼠侵藤我獨傷。鑿石為航癡備息，蒸沙作飯惑全亡，殘經對月看完後，就便和衣臥竹床。人為財名甘受屈，我因智短寄雲豂，喜同瑞獸潛頭角，厭并癡禽惜羽翹。菜圃有肥須數上，粟田無莠亦三穮，所言碌碌非圖富，貴莫閒將歲月消。遯世全真入亂峰，故教名利
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB387.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gusuzun. In a group of mountain-dwelling verses, Gusu Zun pairs carving stone into a boat with steaming sand to make rice and sets both beside lines about folly and delusion disappearing. The speaker pictures impossibilities in poetry while describing a life apart from worldly competition; the verse does not say an actual meal is produced. This local use shares the impossible-transformation image, though the exact relation of the image to the surrounding claims about delusion remains compressed in the poem.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB425.xml). Complete Record of Chan Master Jifei. A questioner asks Jifei Ruyi whether someone may seek awakening without firmly keeping the food and moral precepts. Jifei rejects that advice, then quotes the Surangama Sutra: seeking the path while leaving sexual misconduct, killing, theft and falsehood unrestrained is like steaming sand to make rice, which cannot succeed even after countless ages. Jifei asks what word should be trusted if that scripture is disregarded. The headword is a scriptural image Jifei deploys in his present answer; the questioner and the old scriptural voice remain distinct.

AlternateTargets: make a meal by steaming sand
Senses.Note: The literal impossible operation and its proverbial use remain one sense because every sampled use preserves sand, steaming, and failed rice-making. The later claim that everyone can be fed is an inversion of the same fixed image, not a new referent. The entry preserves that reversal without deciding whether the praise is sincere or ironic.

SearchAliases: make a meal by steaming sand
Zen steam sand to make rice
Senses.Explanation: The records state the failure inside the comparison. One says that seeking outside and blind refining are "like steaming sand to make rice: in the end the matter is not accomplished" (如蒸砂作飯，終不成事). Another asks whether steaming sand to make rice could cure the sore of hunger (譬如蒸砂作飯，豈療飢瘡). It also appears in public interview: an unnamed monk contrasts talking mystery and discussing the old with two futile attempts at nourishment, then asks how a message is passed apart from those roads. One later address by Zhean Jingfan deliberately reverses the fixed impossibility—"steam sand to make rice; everyone can be fed" (蒸砂作飯，人人可飽)—inside praise of the addressed teacher. The Zen corpus therefore uses the impossible meal as criticism, paired proverb, interview premise, and marked inversion.
